sections.h: Sirach 38: the Hebrew behind the Greek
sections.b: The Hebrew of Sirach 38:1-15 survives in manuscript B of the Cairo Genizah, and it is warmer toward doctors than the Greek. It begins, "Make a friend of the doctor before you need him" (38:1, Hebrew). It says, "God brings out remedies from the earth, / and let a man of understanding not reject them" (38:4, Hebrew), the form that Genesis Rabbah 10:6 quotes in Ben Sira's name: "God produced drugs from the earth with which the physician heals the wound, and with which the pharmacist mixes his compounds" (Sefaria's translation). Ben Sira reads the wood that sweetened the water at Marah (Exodus 15:25) as a remedy God placed in creation (38:5). His order for the sick is prayer, repentance and an offering, then the doctor, who also prays for success (38:9-14). At 38:15 the main Hebrew text says the sinner "will act defiantly before the doctor," where the Greek says, "may he fall into a doctor's hands!"

common: Sirach 38 teaches that God heals both through prayer and through doctors and medicines he created.
uncommon: Sirach 38:15 is sometimes read as a joke at doctors' expense; the Hebrew of manuscript B shows it is about the sinner who refuses treatment.

sections.h: Ben Sira's portrait of the scribe
sections.b: Sirach 38:24-39:11 draws a full portrait of the scribe. "A scribe's wisdom comes with the chance of leisure" (38:24): he needs time freed from the plow, the forge and the potter's wheel. He ponders "the law of the Most High," digs out "the wisdom of all the ancients" and "busies himself with prophecies," proverbs and parables (39:1-3). He serves rulers and travels abroad (39:4). He rises at dawn to pray (39:5), and if God wills, "a spirit of understanding will fill him" (39:6). His reward is a name that "will live from generation to generation" (39:9). Ben Sira, who signs his book (50:27), was such a scribe, and his scribe stands between Ezra (Ezra 7:10) and the scribes of the Gospels.

Ben Sira comes back to friendship in Sirach 37:1-6. "Every friend says, 'I am his friend too.' / But a friend can be a friend in name and nothing more" (37:1). It is "a grief that comes close to death / to see a companion and friend become an enemy" (37:2), the same Greek phrase, "grief to death," that Jesus uses in Gethsemane (Mark 14:34). Some companions share the good times and turn away in trouble (37:4). The cure is to choose "a godly man / whom you know keeps the commandments, / whose soul is like your own soul" (37:12), and not to forget a friend when you grow rich (37:6). In the chain of 40:18-27, "A friend and a companion turn up when needed" (40:23), but a good wife is better than both.

Sirach often speaks of death. Death is bitter to the man at ease and welcome to the old and worn out (41:1-2), but it is "the Lord's sentence on all flesh" (41:4), so "Do not be afraid of death's sentence" (41:3). The mourner should weep and bury the dead well, then let grief end, for "there is no way back" (38:21) and grief can kill (38:18). The dead man speaks: "Mine yesterday, and yours today" (38:22). What survives is a good name (41:11-13) and the life of Israel (37:25). Ben Sira says nothing of resurrection. That hope comes in Daniel 12:2, in 2 Maccabees 7 and in the New Testament.

sections.b: Ben Sira's Greek calls the realm of the dead Hades, and the Hebrew of manuscript B has Sheol. "Whether it is ten years or a hundred or a thousand, / in Hades no one argues over the length of a life" (Sirach 41:4). Earlier he says no one in Hades praises the Most High (17:27). This is the older view of Psalm 6:5 and Ecclesiastes 9:10: Sheol ends all striving. The Wisdom of Solomon, in the same Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament, goes further: "the souls of the righteous are in God's hand" in its own wording (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1).

sections.b: Two hymns in Sirach praise creation. The first (39:12-35) answers the complaint that some things are harmful: "The Lord's works, every one of them, are very good" (39:16), the verdict of Genesis 1:31; "No one may say, 'What is this? What is this for?'" (39:17, 21), for each thing has its time and purpose. The second (42:15-43:33) moves through the sky, the weather and the sea, from the sun, "an amazing instrument, the work of the Most High" (43:2), to the rainbow drawn by "the Most High's hands" (43:12), the snow, the frost and the sea monsters. It ends, "the last word is: 'He is the all'" (43:27), and yet God is "the Great One, beyond all his works" (43:28). The Masada scroll, copied in the first century BC, preserves much of the second hymn in Hebrew.

claude.title: The second hymn echoes Genesis 1
claude.body: Claude's suggestion: Sirach 42:15-43:26 begins, as Genesis 1 does, with God's word and moves through the lights of the sky to the creatures of the sea. The fit is loose: the sun comes before the dome of the sky, the weather has no day in Genesis 1, the land and plants are missing, and the rainbow comes from Genesis 9.

sections.h: Ben Sira's answer: everything in its time
sections.b: Sirach 39:16-35 faces harmful things directly: "Some winds were made to punish" (39:28), and fire, hail, famine, wild beasts and the sword "were created to punish" (39:29-30). Ben Sira's answer is that the same things that bless the godly turn to harm for sinners (39:25-27), and that everything will show its worth "in its time" (39:34). In 40:1-11 he admits that toil, fear and bad dreams fall on everyone, from king to beggar, though "seven times more to sinners" (40:8). It is a confident answer, closer to Deuteronomy and Proverbs than to Job.

In the chain of sayings in Sirach 40, "almsgiving remains forever" (40:17), and when brothers and helpers fail, "better than both is almsgiving, which rescues" (40:24). In both places the Hebrew of manuscript B has tsedaqah or tsedeq, "righteousness," the word later Jews used for charity, and the Greek has eleēmosynē. The saying matches Proverbs 10:2, "righteousness rescues from death," and Tobit 12:9, "Alms rescue from death."

Ben Sira's hymn says, "The moon gives the sign for the feasts, / a light that grows smaller when its course is done" (Sirach 43:7). The month is named for the moon (43:8); the Masada scroll plays on Hebrew chodesh, "new moon, month," and mitchaddesh, "renews itself." The sun is praised too (43:2-5), but the calendar of feasts belongs to the moon. This is the calendar of the Jerusalem Temple, against the 364-day sun calendar of 1 Enoch 72-82 and Jubilees.

sections.h: Snow, frost and dew in Ben Sira
sections.b: Sirach 43:13-22 describes winter weather at length. God opens his storehouses and "clouds take wing like birds" (43:14). Snow falls like birds swooping down and settles "the way locusts settle" (43:17); "The eye is struck with wonder at how white and lovely it is" (43:18). Frost is spilled "Like salt" and freezes into points like thorns (43:19); ice covers a pool "like a breastplate" (43:20). Then, after the scorching wind, "A mist brings quick healing to everything" (43:22). Job 37-38 and Psalm 147:16-18 are the closest parallels.

Among the wonders of the sea Ben Sira names "the race of sea monsters" (Sirach 43:25, Greek kētē). The Masada scroll here reads "the might of Rahab," the name of the sea monster that God struck down in Job 26:12 and Isaiah 51:9. In Ben Sira's hymn Rahab is no rebel. It is simply one of the creatures God made and rules, as Leviathan is in Psalm 104:26.

Sirach 38:24-34 describes the plowman, the craftsman and seal-cutter, the smith and the potter. Each "gives his heart" to his work and "lies awake" over it. They have no time for study, so they do not sit as judges or teach in the assembly. Yet "each one is wise in his own work" (38:31), no city could be settled without them (38:32), and "their prayer is in the work of their craft" (38:34). The Egyptian Satire of the Trades also sets the scribe against the hard life of the trades; Egyptologists disagree whether it is meant to mock them. Ben Sira plainly honors them.

The Masada scroll of Ben Sira, copied in the first century BC, writes 'adonai, "Lord," in the creation hymn (Sirach 42:15, 16, 17; 43:5, 10), where the medieval manuscript B has 'elohim, "God," or an abbreviation of the divine name. Ben Sira's Greek translator uses Kyrios, "Lord," and often ho Hypsistos, "the Most High" (37:15; 38:2; 39:1). At 42:17 the Masada Hebrew plays on the title "the LORD of Armies": "Adonai has strengthened his armies."

A chain of sayings in Sirach 40:18-27 ranks the goods of life, each "better than both" of the two before. It ends at the top: "Money and strength make the heart proud, / but better than both is the fear of the Lord. / In the fear of the Lord nothing runs short" (40:26). "The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing" (40:27); the Hebrew of manuscript B says "like an Eden of blessing," with its canopy "over all glory," the words of Isaiah 4:5.

Ben Sira's chain of sayings counts "a blameless wife" better than children and a name (Sirach 40:19), and "a wife with her husband" better than friends (40:23). The Hebrew of manuscript B has "a sensible wife," like Proverbs 19:14. But his advice on daughters is anxious and harsh: a daughter "keeps her father awake in secret" at every stage of life (42:9-10), and "Better a man's wickedness than a woman who does good" (42:14). The Talmud (Sanhedrin 100b) quotes the daughter passage in Ben Sira's name. These lines reflect a society that measured a family's honor by its women.

sections.b: Ben Sira tells the mourner to weep, raise the lament, wrap the body properly "and do not fail to see him buried" (Sirach 38:16), and to mourn "for a day or two, / so that no one can speak against you" (38:17). Then grief must stop, "from grief comes death" (38:18): "You will not help him, and you will hurt yourself" (38:21). Elsewhere he says mourning for the dead lasts seven days (22:12). Tobit, too, counts burial of the dead among the great good works (Tobit 1:17).

Ben Sira warns, "My child, do not live a beggar's life. / It is better to die than to beg" (Sirach 40:28). A man who lives off another's table "lives a life that cannot be counted as living" (40:29). The Talmud (Sanhedrin 100b) quotes a longer saying of Ben Sira on the poor, which the margin of manuscript B also has: "All the days of the poor are evil" (Proverbs 15:15, Hebrew), and "even the nights."
